intro: [PLACEHOLDER] New ethical hackers make these mistakes — avoid them from day one.

mistakes.title: [PLACEHOLDER] Testing without written permission
mistakes.wrong: [PLACEHOLDER] 'I mentioned it verbally and they seemed fine with it.'
mistakes.right: [PLACEHOLDER] Always obtain a signed Statement of Work or Penetration Testing Agreement before touching anything.
mistakes.explanation: [PLACEHOLDER] Verbal agreements are unenforceable and will not protect you if something goes wrong or the client later claims they never authorised testing.

mistakes.title: [PLACEHOLDER] Exceeding the defined scope
mistakes.wrong: [PLACEHOLDER] 'I found an interesting system that wasn't in scope, so I tested it too.'
mistakes.right: [PLACEHOLDER] Immediately stop, document, and notify the client if you discover in-scope systems connecting to out-of-scope systems.
mistakes.explanation: [PLACEHOLDER] Even if the out-of-scope system has critical vulnerabilities, testing it without authorisation is illegal. The scope is a legal boundary.

mistakes.title: [PLACEHOLDER] Confusing a vulnerability scan with a penetration test
mistakes.wrong: [PLACEHOLDER] 'We ran Nessus and got a report — that's our pen test done.'
mistakes.right: [PLACEHOLDER] A vulnerability scan identifies potential issues. A penetration test validates and exploits them to prove real-world impact.
mistakes.explanation: [PLACEHOLDER] A scanner generates many false positives and tells you nothing about actual exploitability. Manual testing and exploitation proof are what deliver real value.
mistakes.example: [PLACEHOLDER] A scanner might report a web server version as vulnerable to a 2019 CVE. A pen tester would confirm whether the specific configuration is actually exploitable.
